With both liquefaction trains producing at full capacity it would take approximately 10.2 hours to fill one unit to 90% capacity, and it would take 3 days to produce a full 20,000 m³ cargo of liquid CO (the intended capacity 2 of the dedicated CO ship). 2 The option of storing liquid CO in spheres was considered. This would produce the minimum number of 2 vessels, however they would require significant site fabrication and will likely drive the project duration. This option was therefore not progressed further in this phase but can be revisited in future phases. During subsequent project phases heat gain calculations will be conducted to optimize the insulation thickness. As a benchmark reference European projects indicate that approximately 100mm of insulation has allowed 5 days holding time with no venting at 20°C ambient. For T-RICH’s tanks, 200mm has been conservatively assumed until the calculations are complete. Facilities will be included in the design for recirculating liquid CO into and out of the tanks as this might 2 be necessary for operational reasons (e.g. to avoid stratified layers in the tank.) Should US fabrication be essential, then Option 2 can be progressed within the existing site by expanding the storage area to the East. This will limit the ability to expand storage in the future if additional compression / liquefaction trains are developed to increase throughput. The cost of transporting the 11 insulated vessels from Spain to Florida has been investigated and included in the evaluation. Preliminary indications from in-house shipping experts is that these tanks can be transferred in a single shipment using for example a Rolldock ST class heavy lift Ro-Ro multipurpose dry cargo ship. The transit would take approximately 3 days at a cost of several million USD. This additional cost and duration is not sufficient to sway the decision regarding revised base case as the Total Installed Cost differential is in excess of 41 Million USD. Figure 4.27 – Example Heavy Lift Vessel for Shipping Storage Tanks from Spain to Tampa Spherical tanks were also considered in a separate analysis. Such tanks have several advantages for holding cold, pressurized liquids like liquified CO which is why they are often used to store liquefied 2 petroleum gas (LPG) on land. First, due to their shape, stress concentrations are minimized and the stress in the steel shell is uniform over the entire surface of the tank. Second, spheres have the lowest surface area for a given volume of any other tank shape. This presents a particular advantage with low- Page89 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version temperature liquids since it limits the surface area of the tank through which heat can enter the tank, raise the temperature of the liquid and create boil-off gas which raises the pressure inside the tank and increases the risk of loss of containment. As a corollary, that minimizes the amount of thermal insulation that must be installed on the tank surface, minimizing initial and future maintenance costs.
